questions.stem: Poly(ethene) is made from ethene monomers. A student draws the repeating unit with a C=C double bond still present. What is wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing is wrong; the double bond remains in the polymer
The double bond opens up during polymerisation, so the repeating unit should show only single C-C bonds
The repeating unit should show a triple bond
Poly(ethene) is not made from ethene

questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond in each monomer opens up so that one bond links to the next monomer. The repeating unit of poly(ethene) is -CH₂-CH₂- with only single bonds. If you see the monomer CH₂=CH₂, the polymer repeating unit shows the bond opened: -(CH₂-CH₂)ₙ-.

questions.stem: PVC (poly(chloroethene)) is used for window frames and pipes, while poly(ethene) is used for plastic bags. Both are addition polymers. What structural difference gives PVC its greater rigidity?

options.text: PVC has chlorine atoms attached to the chain, which create stronger intermolecular forces between chains and restrict movement
PVC has shorter chains than poly(ethene)
PVC is made from alkanes while poly(ethene) is made from alkenes
PVC contains double bonds that make it more rigid

questions.explanation: PVC's monomer (chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl) has a chlorine atom that remains in the polymer chain. The C-Cl bond is polar, creating stronger dipole-dipole intermolecular forces between polymer chains compared to the non-polar poly(ethene). These stronger forces make PVC more rigid and harder, which is why it is used for structural applications like window frames.

questions.stem: A major environmental problem with addition polymers like poly(ethene) is that they persist in the environment. Why are they so resistant to decomposition?

options.text: They are too small for microorganisms to break down
The strong C-C backbone is non-biodegradable because most microorganisms lack enzymes to break these bonds
They dissolve in rainwater and wash away before decomposing
They react with oxygen in the air and become even more stable

questions.explanation: Addition polymers have a backbone of strong, non-polar C-C single bonds. Most microorganisms and their enzymes cannot break these bonds, so the polymers are non-biodegradable. They can persist in landfill sites and the environment for hundreds of years. This is why recycling, reducing plastic use, and developing biodegradable alternatives are important.

questions.stem: Given the monomer propene (CH₂=CHCH₃), what would the repeating unit of poly(propene) look like?

options.text: -(CH₂-CHCH₃)ₙ- with the CH₃ group branching off the main chain
-(CH₂=CHCH₃)ₙ- with the double bond intact
-(CH₂-CH₂-CH₃)ₙ- as a straight chain
-(CH₃-CH₃)ₙ- with the CH₂ group removed

questions.explanation: When propene undergoes addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond opens up, but the CH₃ group remains attached to one of the carbons. The repeating unit is -(CH₂-CH(CH₃))ₙ-, where the methyl group branches off the main chain. This branch affects the polymer's properties — poly(propene) is stronger and stiffer than poly(ethene).

questions.stem: PTFE (poly(tetrafluoroethene), commonly known as Teflon) is used to coat non-stick frying pans. Its monomer is CF₂=CF₂. Why is PTFE so chemically resistant and slippery?

options.text: It contains carbon-carbon double bonds that repel other molecules
The strong C-F bonds are very difficult to break, and the fluorine atoms create extremely weak intermolecular forces with other substances
PTFE is a liquid at cooking temperatures, so food slides off
PTFE is a metal alloy that is naturally smooth

questions.explanation: C-F bonds are among the strongest single bonds in organic chemistry, making PTFE extremely chemically resistant. The fluorine atoms surrounding the carbon chain create a surface with very weak intermolecular forces with other substances, so almost nothing sticks to it. This combination of chemical resistance and non-stick properties makes PTFE ideal for cookware coatings.
